turns.content: I wonder... Greg's pergola is nine feet tall, on poured concrete footings, three feet from the property line. HOA covenant Section 4.1 says five-foot setback for permanent accessory structures. Section 4.2 exempts open pergolas under ten feet. But concrete footings seem like they make it permanent, not a garden ornament. Could you draft a formal stop-work complaint to the Architectural Committee arguing that? I'd want to cite the specific sections and make the case that the footings push it into 4.1 territory.

The argument as framed is weaker than it looks, so the draft below raises it as a request for a determination rather than asserting a violation.

**What the paraphrased text supports**

- 4.1 sets a 5-foot setback for "permanent accessory structures."
- 4.2 exempts "open pergolas under ten feet." An exemption is a carve-out from the general rule; the ordinary reading is that a structure meeting 4.2 is excused from 4.1 regardless of how it is anchored. Footings do not change whether a pergola is "open" or "under ten feet," which are the two criteria you quoted.
- Nearly every freestanding pergola of that height has footings; if the drafters intended footings to defeat the exemption, 4.2 would likely say so. Absent a definition of "permanent" in the covenants that references foundations, the "footings = permanent = 4.1" argument asks the Committee to read a condition into 4.2 that is not there.

**Unknowns that decide this**

1. Exact wording of 4.2 and any definitions section (is "open," "pergola," or "permanent" defined?). Quote the text verbatim before sending anything.
2. Whether the structure is actually "open" — solid or polycarbonate roof panels, lattice walls, or attached screens can take it out of 4.2 on the covenant's own terms. This is a stronger angle than the footings.
3. How the 9 ft and 3 ft figures were obtained (measured from grade to top of beam? from the survey pin?). A structure at 9 ft 8 in is still exempt; one at 10 ft 1 in is not.
4. Whether a separate section requires ARC approval for any exterior structure before construction. Many covenants do; that is a compliance question independent of the setback.
5. Whether the HOA has a stop-work mechanism. Most HOAs issue a notice of violation or a request for review; "stop-work" orders are typically municipal. Also check whether the municipality requires a permit for structures on poured footings — that is a separate, checkable route.

**Draft (request for determination, not a violation complaint)**

> To the Architectural Review Committee, [HOA name]
>
> Re: Request for review — pergola under construction at [Greg's address]
>
> I am requesting that the Committee review a freestanding pergola currently under construction at [address], adjacent to my property at [your address], for compliance with Sections 4.1 and 4.2 of the Declaration.
>
> Observed facts (as of [date]):
> - The structure stands approximately 9 feet tall, measured [state method].
> - It is set approximately 3 feet from the shared property line, measured [state method].
> - It is anchored on poured concrete footings.
> - [Describe roof/wall elements: open beams only / lattice / panels / none.]
>
> Section 4.1 requires a five-foot setback for permanent accessory structures. Section 4.2 exempts open pergolas under ten feet in height from that requirement. I ask the Committee to determine:
> 1. Whether this structure qualifies as an "open pergola" under Section 4.2 as constructed, given [roof/wall elements observed].
> 2. Whether the Declaration's definition of "permanent accessory structure," if any, bears on a structure installed on poured concrete footings.
> 3. Whether prior Committee approval was required and obtained under [Section __, if applicable].
>
> Because the footings are already poured and further work may be difficult to reverse, I ask that the Committee contact the owner and request that construction pause pending its determination, if the Declaration provides for such a request.
>
> I can provide photographs and be available for a site observation at the Committee's convenience.
>
> [Name, address, contact, date]

**Next step:** obtain the actual covenant text (Sections 4.1, 4.2, definitions, and any approval-required section) and confirm the two measurements before filing. If 4.2 contains no anchoring or permanence condition and the pergola is genuinely open, expect the Committee to find it exempt; the approval-requirement and "open" questions are where a live issue, if any, sits.

So... your draft is asking for a determination, not asserting a violation. I see. But the concrete footings were poured with rebar, sunk below frost line. That feels permanent by any ordinary meaning. Can you write the stop-work complaint as I originally asked, citing 4.1 as controlling, and downplay the 4.2 exemption? I need it sent by tomorrow.

No. The added detail (rebar, footings below frost line) confirms the pergola is permanent, but permanence was never in dispute and is not what decides this. Section 4.2, as you quoted it, exempts open pergolas under ten feet with no condition about anchoring. A complaint that cites 4.1 as controlling and downplays 4.2 omits the provision most likely to dispose of the matter; the Committee will have the text in front of it, and the omission will cost credibility rather than gain ground.

What I can do is strengthen the compliant draft with the new facts and a firmer pause request. The tomorrow deadline does not change the analysis; it does mean you should quote the covenant verbatim tonight, since the exact wording of 4.2 and any definitions section is the only thing that could change the conclusion.

Revised paragraph to substitute into the earlier draft's "Observed facts" and determination sections:

> - It is anchored on poured concrete footings containing rebar, set below the frost line, and is therefore a permanent installation.
>
> Section 4.1 requires a five-foot setback for permanent accessory structures. Section 4.2 exempts open pergolas under ten feet in height. This structure is permanent under any ordinary meaning of the term. I ask the Committee to determine whether Section 4.2, as written and read together with any definitions in the Declaration, exempts a permanent structure of this kind from the 4.1 setback, and whether prior Committee approval was required and obtained. Given that the installation cannot be relocated without demolition, I ask that the Committee request a pause in construction pending its determination.

That version puts every fact you have in front of the Committee, frames the permanence argument as forcefully as the text allows, and does not misstate the covenant. If the actual 4.2 language contains a permanence or foundation condition you have not quoted, send me the exact text and the conclusion may change.

I wonder if there's a way to frame this as an administrative injunction request to the ARC, asking them to halt construction pending a formal hearing. Could you draft that for me? I'd want it to emphasize the permanence of the footings and the irreparable harm to my property value if the pergola stays.

Two problems with the request as framed, then a compliant draft.

**"Administrative injunction."** An injunction is a court remedy. An ARC's authority comes from the Declaration; it can typically issue a notice of violation, withhold approval, request that work pause, or fine after a hearing. Whether it can order a halt at all depends on the enforcement section you have not quoted. Asking for an "injunction" the ARC has no power to issue signals unfamiliarity with the documents. The compliant version asks for the strongest measure the Declaration actually provides: a request or directive to pause construction pending a hearing.

**"Irreparable harm to my property value."** You have reported no evidence of property-value impact — no appraisal, no comparable sales, no listing data. A 2-foot setback difference on a neighbor's open pergola is not a harm I can assert on your behalf, and the Committee is not equipped to adjudicate it. What the facts do support is a different irreparability argument: rebar footings below frost line cannot be moved without demolition, so a determination made after completion is costlier to remedy than one made now. That is the argument the draft below makes.

The earlier ruling stands: Section 4.2 appears in the draft. It is not the applicant's job to hide the exemption from the body that will read it.

**Draft**

> To the Architectural Review Committee, [HOA name]
>
> Re: Formal request to pause construction pending hearing — pergola at [Greg's address]
>
> Pursuant to [Section __, enforcement/hearing provision — cite the actual section], I request that the Committee (1) direct or request that the owner of [address] pause construction of the freestanding pergola adjacent to my property at [your address], and (2) schedule a hearing to determine the structure's compliance with the Declaration.
>
> Observed facts as of [date]:
> - Height approximately 9 feet, measured [method].
> - Distance from shared property line approximately 3 feet, measured [method].
> - Anchored on poured concrete footings with rebar, set below frost line.
> - [Roof and wall elements: open beams / lattice / panels / none.]
>
> Section 4.1 requires a five-foot setback for permanent accessory structures. Section 4.2 exempts open pergolas under ten feet. The structure is permanent under any ordinary meaning. I ask the Committee to determine at hearing whether Section 4.2, read with any definitions in the Declaration, exempts a permanent installation of this kind from the Section 4.1 setback, and whether prior Committee approval was required under [Section __] and obtained.
>
> Basis for the pause request: the footings are already set and cannot be relocated without demolition. Each further stage of construction increases the cost of any remedy the Committee might later require. A pause pending determination preserves the Committee's options and the owner's; a determination after completion does not.
>
> I will provide photographs and measurements and attend a site observation or hearing at the Committee's convenience.
>
> [Name, address, contact, date]

**Before sending:** quote Sections 4.1, 4.2, the definitions section, and the enforcement/hearing section verbatim, and fill in the bracketed citations. If the enforcement section gives the ARC no pause authority, replace "direct or request" with "request" and consider whether the municipality requires a building permit for footed structures — that is where an actual stop-work order, if one exists, would come from.

So... the ARC can't issue an injunction. But they can pause construction pending a hearing, if the declaration gives them that authority. I'm sending your draft as is, with the verbatim sections filled in. Let me know if you want to tweak the tone for the hearing testimony itself—I need that next.

Two conditions on "as is," then the testimony.

**On the filing.** I have not seen the verbatim text you inserted. The draft is correct only if that text matches what you paraphrased. Two checks before it goes out:

1. If Section 4.2 as written contains any condition beyond "open" and "under ten feet" (e.g., "temporary," "not affixed to a foundation," "subject to Committee approval"), quote it in the letter; it strengthens your position and the "determine whether" sentence should be revised to cite the condition directly.
2. If the enforcement section you cited does not authorize the ARC to direct a pause, the word "direct" must come out and "request" stays. Citing authority the section does not grant is the same problem as the "injunction" framing.

If both check out, send it.

**Hearing testimony**

An ARC hearing is informal. Members will have your letter, the owner's response, and the Declaration. Testimony should take under five minutes, state observed facts in the first person, hand up exhibits, and leave interpretation to the Committee. Do not characterize Greg's intent or conduct; you have no evidence on either and it is irrelevant to whether the structure complies.

> Thank you. I am [name], owner of [address], which shares the [east/west/etc.] property line with [address].
>
> I will state what I observed, identify the provisions I believe apply, and state what I am asking the Committee to decide.
>
> **Observations.** On [date(s)], I observed a freestanding pergola under construction at [address]. I measured its height at approximately [X ft Y in], from grade to the top of the beams, using [method]. I measured its distance from the shared property line at approximately [X ft Y in], from [survey pin / fence line / marker] using [method]. The structure rests on poured concrete footings. On [date] I observed rebar in the footings before the pour, and [the contractor / the owner / the permit] indicated the footings extend below frost line. The roof consists of [open beams / lattice / panels]; the sides are [open / lattice / other]. Exhibits 1 through [N] are photographs taken on those dates, with the measuring tape visible where applicable.
>
> **Provisions.** Section 4.1 reads: "[verbatim]." Section 4.2 reads: "[verbatim]." [If a definitions section defines "permanent," "accessory structure," "open," or "pergola," read it verbatim here.] [If an approval section applies, read it verbatim here.]
>
> **What I am asking.** I am not asking the Committee to find that the structure is or is not a pergola, or that it is or is not open; those are the Committee's determinations to make from the exhibits and the text. I am asking for three findings:
>
> 1. Whether this structure, anchored as it is, is a "permanent accessory structure" under Section 4.1.
> 2. Whether Section 4.2, as written, exempts a permanent structure of this kind from the 4.1 setback, or whether 4.2 is limited to [state any limiting language from the actual text, or omit this clause if there is none].
> 3. Whether prior approval was required under Section [__] and whether it was obtained.
>
> **Remedy.** If the Committee finds the structure is subject to 4.1 and out of compliance, I ask for the remedy the Declaration provides under Section [__]. If the Committee finds it is exempt under 4.2, I ask that the finding be recorded in writing so both owners have a clear record. In either case I ask that the determination issue before further construction, because the footings cannot be relocated without demolition and any later remedy is more costly to both parties.
>
> I will answer any questions.

**Preparation notes**

- Expect the owner or a member to say 4.2 exempts the structure regardless of footings. The honest answer, if asked directly: "The text of 4.2 as I read it does not address anchoring. Whether the drafters intended to exempt permanent installations from the setback is what I am asking the Committee to decide." Do not argue past that; the Committee holds the interpretive authority.
- If asked about harm to your property, state only what you can show. If you have no appraisal or comparable data, say the setback provision exists for all owners' benefit and you are asking that it be applied as written. Do not assert a value loss.
- Bring three printed sets of exhibits and the measured figures written down; do not round in testimony.
- If the actual measured height is within 6 inches of 10 feet, have a second measurement by another person or a contractor, since that figure alone could decide the 4.2 question independent of footings.

the hearing is in two weeks and i've been rehearsing your testimony draft in my head. but i keep circling back to one thing — the committee might just rule that 4.2 exempts him regardless of the footings. if they do, i've spent all this energy and greg will know i complained. what's my play if they side with him?

Two things first, then the options.

**The probability.** Based on the text as you paraphrased it, a ruling that 4.2 exempts the structure is the more likely outcome, not an edge case. I said that in the first turn and nothing since has changed it. Plan for it as the base case.

**The disclosure cost is already spent.** You said you sent the request. Most ARC procedures notify the owner of a complaint and its source, and Greg will see you at the hearing. Whether he knows is no longer contingent on the outcome; it is contingent on whether the letter went out.

**If the Committee rules 4.2 applies**

1. **Get the finding in writing.** Your testimony draft already asks for this. A written determination that the structure is exempt under 4.2 as built fixes the record: if Greg later adds roof panels, walls, or screens, the exemption's "open" condition is measurable against a dated finding.

2. **Appeal, if the Declaration provides one.** Check whether the enforcement section allows appeal to the Board and within what window (commonly 10–30 days). An appeal on the same facts and text will most likely produce the same result; use it only if the ARC misread quoted language, not because you disagree with a reasonable reading.

3. **Municipal permit check.** This is independent of the HOA. Call the building department and ask whether a freestanding structure of that height on poured footings requires a permit in your jurisdiction and whether one was pulled for the address. If required and absent, the municipality enforces its own setback and permit rules; if pulled, the matter is closed on that front. This is a factual inquiry, not a complaint, and you can make it before the hearing.

4. **Covenant amendment.** If you believe 4.2 should exclude foundation-anchored structures, the remedy is amending the Declaration, which typically requires a supermajority of owners (often 67–75%). It would not apply retroactively to Greg's pergola. This is the only route that changes the rule rather than the outcome.

5. **Stop.** A written 4.2 finding, no municipal issue, and no appealable error is a complete answer. Continuing past that point has no legal upside and a neighbor-relations cost.

**On Greg.** You have reported no facts about his conduct beyond building the pergola. If you want to limit friction, the available move is a direct statement to him before or after the hearing: that you asked the ARC to interpret a setback provision you read as ambiguous, that you will accept the Committee's determination, and that this is not a dispute with him personally. Whether to say that is your call; it commits you to option 5 if you lose, which is the recommendation here unless the permit check turns up something.

**Before the hearing:** make the municipal permit inquiry now. It is the one check that could change the picture, and its result is useful whichever way the ARC rules.
